newsitem.title: UK: UK gilts still under cosh despite auction success.
newsitem.headline: UK gilts still under cosh despite auction success.

text.p: Ample cover at the 3.0 billion stg auction of ultra-long gilts brought a little comfort to the troubled UK government debt market, but analysts said the result does not herald a reverse of gilts' recent underperformance.

"The convergence story seem to be driving European bonds at the moment and since the UK is not part of that there is not much chance of an early narrowing of the spread," said Kevin Adams, gilts analyst at BZW.
The auction of 8.0 percent gilts due 2021 was covered 1.73 times and had a yield tail of two basis points.
Ultra-long gilts provide a good match for the liabilities of domestic pension funds and insurance companies. They generated much of the demand at the auction.

"The maturity means it's really one for domestic investors. Overseas investors were not heavily involved," said Adams. "And it's worth bearing in mind that domestic institutional investors are sitting on a lot of cash which is supporting gilts."
But a growing feeling on European bond markets that monetary union is forging ahead, helped by last weekend's Ecofin meeting, has left gilts slightly sidelined as the convergence story takes root.
The yield spread against Bunds stood at 181 basis points after the auction compared with 165 only four weeks ago.
Swedish bonds now trade substantially through gilts at 10-years with Spanish bonds closing fast.
Don Smith, international bond strategist at HSBC Markets, said there is not much prospect of gilts making back ground near-term.
"Over the next two or three months its difficult to see any factors leading to a narrowing of the spread."
But long-term, a change of government may offer hope, he said.

"Looking further ahead, there is scope for the spread to narrow considerably on the assumption that the Labour Party forms the next government and markets become more optimsitic that sterling will be part of EMU," said Smith.
The Labour Party is widely perceived to be more pro-EMU than the ruling Conservatives.

Both parties are committed to having a referendum on Britain signing up to EMU, but the Labour party will do so only of it believes the country has not already been adeqately consulted at an election.
But few economists expect the spread against Bunds to widen much further.
"The only thing that could prompt that is if (Chancellor of the Exchequer Kenneth) Clarke resigned," said Adams.
Rumours swirled around the futures' pits on Tuesday that he would resign over the party's squabble on EMU. But the talk was flatly denied by the Treasury.
"Any new Chancellor would be seen as less likely to wear a hair-shirt at budget time which would frighten gilts," said Adams.
